title: Is Ownership Right for You? A Capital & Readiness Checklist
section: Part Two · Module 0 - Ownership vs. Arbitrage

slides.kicker: Part Two · Module 0 · Ownership vs. Arbitrage
slides.title: The down payment is the smallest question; fund the full stack before you shop
slides.subtitle: Lesson 0.3. Is Ownership Right for You? A Capital & Readiness Checklist
meta: Education only. Not legal, tax, lending, or financial advice.
slides.notes:
This lesson answers one question before you look at a single listing. Can you actually afford to own?

By the end, you'll be able to add up the full cash an ownership deal needs, not just the down payment. You'll compare it with the money you really have, after you keep your own emergency savings. You'll test whether you'd survive a delayed opening or a weak first season. And you'll finish with a one-page readiness scorecard.

That scorecard sends you to one of four places. PA.1, the next lesson, where you write your buy box. Better financing or liquidity first. The Part One lease path, where you rent a place and host it instead of buying. Or wait.

I'll run one example couple, Maya and Chris, through all of it. You'll meet them on the next slide. On the surface they look very ready. You'll see where that changes. Every Cedar Ridge figure is an assumption from the course example file, and new ones are marked.

Hearing "not yet" here is much cheaper than hearing it at a closing table.

slides.title: Maya and Chris bring $210,000 of savings and two loan quotes to a $385,000 house
rows: Maya and Chris: two earners, $185,000 income, credit scores around 740
3-bedroom lake-market house, not their main home; about 10 personal days a year
7.25%, 1 point, PITIA $2,557 a month; qualifies mainly on the property's income
6.875%, no points, PITIA $2,484 a month; qualifies on household income and debts
About 212 nights a year, 61 stays, $300 average nightly rate (ADR)
slides.caption: DSCR means debt service coverage ratio. A point is an upfront fee equal to 1% of the loan, paid for a lower rate.
slides.notes:
Before we do any math, meet the people and the house. Everything here is hypothetical, from the course example file.

Maya and Chris are a two-earner household. They make $185,000 combined, and their credit scores are around 740. They have $210,000 in liquid savings outside retirement. They also own their home, worth $520,000 with a $260,000 mortgage.

They're buying Cedar Ridge, a three-bedroom house in a lake market about two hours from a city. The price is $385,000 with 25% down. It's a short-term rental they'll also use about 10 days a year. It isn't their main home.

They have two loan quotes. A DSCR loan, short for debt service coverage ratio, qualifies mainly on the property's income against its payment. A conventional loan qualifies on their household income and debts. The DSCR quote carries one point. A point is an upfront fee of 1% of the loan, paid for a lower rate.

In the example, the house books about 212 nights a year across 61 stays, at $300 a night on average.

slides.eyebrow: The first number most buyers check
slides.title: A $96,250 down payment against $210,000 saved looks ready twice over
slides.text: $96,250 down against $210,000 saved looks ready twice over. The full bill says otherwise.
slides.support: Closing, furnishing, repairs, permits, the months before the first guest, a reserve for the house, and a reserve for your own household.
slides.notes:
Most buyers start with one number: the down payment. For Cedar Ridge, 25% of $385,000 is $96,250. Maya and Chris have $210,000 in liquid savings outside retirement accounts. On that math alone, they could make the down payment twice.

That math leaves out most of the bill.

An owned short-term rental needs money for closing, furnishing, repairs, and permits. It needs money for the months before the first guest arrives. It needs reserves, for the lender and for you. And your own household has to stay safe if the house has a bad year.

So in this lesson I lay out every layer, one at a time. Then we run Maya and Chris through it and see what's left.

Keep the $210,000 in your head. We'll come back to it, and by the end the answer won't be "twice over". It'll be a gap.

slides.title: The cash stack has eight layers: six you spend and two you must still hold
slides.keyline: A common failure is counting the same dollars as the house reserve and the family's emergency fund.
rows: Lender fees, title, escrow, prepaid items, discount points
Furniture, linens, kitchen, safety equipment, photos
Inspection findings you'll fix yourself after closing, plus work before guests
Loan payment, utilities, software, retainers before the first booking
The lender's required reserves, then your operating cushion
Your household's own safety net, separate from the house
slides.notes:
Think of the cash requirement as a stack of eight layers. The order doesn't change the total. You need all of them funded. If you don't, you're counting on the house to perform from day one.

Layers 1 to 6 are money you'll spend. First come the down payment, closing costs and points, and furnishing. Then the repair and safety punch list, permits and inspections, and the carrying costs before the first booking. That last one catches people. The loan payment starts whether or not a guest has booked.

Layers 7 and 8 are money you must still have after spending all that. Layer 7 is the property reserve. The lender may require it to make the loan, and after closing it becomes your cushion for the house. Layer 8 is your household's own emergency savings.

A common failure is merging 7 and 8. A buyer counts the same dollars twice, once for the house and once for the family. Then the water heater fails in the same month a paycheck is late. And there's one pile of cash for two problems.

slides.title: Count only liquid savings; retirement, HELOC, gift, and seller money have conditions

left.head: Counts in this lesson
left.note: Checking, savings, and taxable brokerage accounts.
items: The cleanest source. Lenders usually want to see where it came from and how long it's been there.
Ask your lender what documentation they need for large recent deposits.

right.head: Borrowed or conditional
right.note: Ask your lender and CPA before you count any of these.
items: Retirement: some lenders may count part toward reserves; withdrawals can carry tax and penalties.
HELOC: usually a variable rate, and your home is the collateral ([CFPB](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/ask-cfpb/what-is-a-home-equity-line-of-credit-heloc-en-107/)).
Gifts or partners: lender rules apply; ownership and loan papers must match (PA.10).
Seller concessions: a negotiation item for PA.8 (offers), not money to count now.

slides.notes:
Money for the stack can come from several places. Each one has limits, and your lender may treat them differently. In this lesson, we count only liquid savings.

Liquid savings are the cleanest. That's checking, savings, and taxable brokerage. Lenders usually want to see where it came from and how long it's been there.

Retirement accounts are different. Some lenders may count part of a retirement balance toward reserves. But withdrawals can carry taxes and penalties. Ask your lender and CPA.

Home equity looks tempting. Maya and Chris have $260,000 of equity on paper. A HELOC lets them borrow against it. The CFPB notes that HELOCs usually carry a variable rate, and your home is the collateral. A HELOC is borrowed money, not savings, and it adds a payment. OP.11 covers HELOCs for scaling.

Gifts and partner money follow lender rules, and the ownership paperwork has to match (PA.10). A seller may pay part of closing costs, but that's a negotiation later (PA.8), not money to count now.

If the stack only works with borrowed money, write that down as a finding.

slides.title: The lender's reserve rule is a floor to get the loan, not a plan for a bad season
items: Fannie Mae measures reserves in months of the new loan's PITIA ([Selling Guide B3-4.1-01](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-4.1-01/minimum-reserve-requirements)).
No minimum for a one-unit principal residence. Cedar Ridge isn't their main home, so that rule doesn't apply.
Owning other financed properties can add more. For Maya and Chris, likely zero; their lender confirms.
DSCR lenders set their own rule. Get each lender's number in writing (PA.6, PA.7).

box.label: For teaching: 6 months of PITIA (assumption)
box.text: DSCR quote: 6 x $2,557 = **$15,342**. Conventional quote: 6 x $2,484 = **$14,904**.

slides.notes:
Lenders measure reserves in months of the new loan's payment. That payment is principal, interest, taxes, insurance, and association dues. People shorten it to PITIA.

Fannie Mae's Selling Guide lays out the rules for loans it buys. There's no minimum for a one-unit principal residence. Second homes and investment properties do have requirements. Cedar Ridge isn't Maya and Chris's main home, so the no-minimum rule doesn't apply. Their lender decides which category it falls in.

If you already own other financed properties besides your home, lenders can require extra reserves. For Maya and Chris that add-on is likely zero. Their lender confirms it.

The DSCR quote isn't a Fannie Mae loan. Each DSCR lender sets its own rule. For teaching I assume 6 months: $15,342 on the DSCR quote, $14,904 on the conventional.

After closing, the lender stops watching. That reserve becomes your cushion. The lender's number is a floor, not a plan.

slides.title: With no STR income counted, Maya and Chris's illustrative DTI is 35.6%
slides.text: Credit: around 740. Each lender sets its own minimum and prices the rate by score. A conventional lender also checks debts against income (DTI).
rows: DTI with no STR income counted
slides.caption: Ask each lender for its maximum DTI and write it next to yours. For your own budget, the DSCR payment of $2,557 gives 36.0%. A DSCR lender checks a coverage ratio instead: 1.18 to 2.42 in the course example, by the lender's definition (PA.6).
slides.notes:
Besides cash, three things shape whether a lender will lend: credit, loan type, and debt capacity.

Credit first. Maya and Chris have scores around 740. Each lender sets its own minimum and prices its rate by score. Kiavi's DSCR guide, for example, says it looks at credit score and down payment, not only coverage. That's one lender, not a market standard.

Then the loan type. Fannie Mae's Selling Guide has a section on short-term rental income from the property being bought. Whether a lender counts that income for you is their call. PA.7 compares the paths.

Then debt capacity. Monthly income is $15,417. Their home payment and other debts are assumptions, $2,400 and $600. Add the $2,484 conventional PITIA, and debts total $5,484. That's 35.6% of income, with no rental income counted. Is that high? Only the lender's maximum tells you, so ask for it in writing.

A DSCR lender checks a coverage ratio instead: property income over PITIA. In the course example it runs from 1.18 to 2.42, depending on the lender's definition. PA.6 walks through it.

slides.title: Each month between closing and the first guest costs $3,257 with nothing coming in
slides.side:
The base stack already includes **2 months** (assumption): $6,514.

A **3-month delay** beyond that adds 3 x $3,257 = **$9,771**.

side_box.label: What causes it
side_box.text: Permits take longer. Furniture arrives late. A contractor misses a week.

slides.notes:
Two things go wrong often enough that you should budget for both. The first is a delayed opening.

Permits take longer than expected. Furniture arrives late. A contractor misses a week. Every month between closing and the first guest costs the full carrying cost, with no revenue.

For Cedar Ridge on the DSCR quote, that's $3,257 a month. It's the $2,557 PITIA, plus the example's $450 of utilities, $100 of software, and $150 for the handyman retainer.

The base stack already includes two months of carrying costs as an assumption. That's $6,514. Now suppose you get three more months of delay on top of that. That's another $9,771.

Where does that money come from? Not from the house. The house isn't earning yet. It comes from the property reserve, and if that's not enough, from your household.

When you build your own stack, don't use the fastest timeline anyone's quoted you. Ask the permit office for real processing times. Ask the furniture vendor for realistic delivery dates.

slides.title: A 3-month delay plus one weak year leaves $96 of the $15,342 reserve
slides.caption: Weak case: average nightly rate (ADR) $265, 50% occupancy. It loses $5,475 a year on the DSCR quote, after the loan payment and all operating costs.

box.label: Plan for the pair
box.text: It's the kind of pairing that can force a sale at a bad time. Their own reserve target covers it: $9,771 + $5,475 = **$15,246** (assumption).

slides.notes:
The second thing is a weak first season. A new listing has no reviews. It may book below its long-run potential for a while.

The example's weak case is $265 a night at 50% occupancy. On the DSCR quote it loses $5,475 a year. That's after the loan payment and all operating costs. On its own, the $15,342 reserve would cover about 2.8 years of that loss.

But look at what happens when both hit. Start with the $15,342 reserve. A three-month delay takes $9,771. That leaves $5,571. Then a weak first year loses $5,475. That leaves $96.

That's the pairing I want you to plan for. It's the kind that can force a sale at a bad time, because the cushion runs out when the house is weakest.

So Maya and Chris set their own reserve target to survive it: $15,246. The six-month lender figure just covers it, with $96 to spare. You'll see that on line 3 of their scorecard.

slides.title: Self-managing Cedar Ridge takes about 140 hours a year, and the cleaner may log more
items: 1.5 hours per stay x 61 stays (the example's stays a year) = 91.5 hours on messages, scheduling, and checks.
4 hours a month x 12 = 48 hours on bookkeeping, pricing, and vendor calls.
About 140 hours a year, or 2.7 hours a week. Some weeks bring an 11 p.m. lockout.
A cleaner at 4 hours x 61 turnovers logs 244 hours. IRS participation tests compare your hours with others' ([Pub 925](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p925)); see 0.2.
A co-host charging 18% of booking revenue turned base-case cash flow from $5,572 to -$7,798 in 0.2.
slides.notes:
Cash isn't the only resource. Owning also takes time, and a stomach for ups and downs.

In the base case, Maya and Chris self-manage with a local cleaner and an on-call handyman. Assume 1.5 hours per stay on messages, scheduling, and turnover checks. With the example's 61 stays, that's 91.5 hours. Add 4 hours a month on bookkeeping, pricing, and vendor calls. That's 48 more. Together, about 140 hours a year, or 2.7 hours a week.

That hour count matters for taxes too. A rental can show a paper loss. Whether that loss is usable against your other income can depend on material participation. That's a set of IRS tests about how involved you are, and 0.2 covers it. Publication 925's tests compare your hours with other people's, like the cleaner's. At 4 hours on each of 61 turnovers, the cleaner logs 244 hours. That's more than the owners' 140. Your CPA confirms how your hours count.

The alternative is a co-host. In 0.2, one charging 18% of booking revenue sank the base case to minus $7,798.

slides.title: Ten personal days stay under the IRS limit; the harder test is living with -$27,503

left.head: Personal use
left.note: Maya and Chris plan about 10 days a year.
items: Pub 527: used as a home if personal days exceed the greater of 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days ([IRS](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p527)).
Counting 212 rented nights as fair-rental days, the threshold is 21.2 days. Ten is below it; CPA confirms.
Ten nights at the $300 base average nightly rate (ADR) are worth up to $3,000. Stay in slow weeks.

right.head: Risk tolerance
right.note: The five-year test from 0.2: cash flow plus sale proceeds, against the $142,688 put in. Before tax.
items: Base case: $27,732 ahead.
Weak case: $27,503 behind.
If either owner's honest answer is no, that's a readiness result, and a useful one.

slides.notes:
Two more resources: your own calendar, and your nerves.

Personal use first. Maya and Chris plan about 10 personal days a year. IRS Publication 527 treats a dwelling as used as a home if personal use passes a threshold. The threshold is the greater of 14 days or 10% of fair-rental days. It also requires dividing expenses by days. Counting 212 rented nights as fair-rental days, the threshold is 21.2 days. So 10 days is below it, and the CPA confirms the count.

There's also a revenue cost. Those 10 nights at the $300 base rate are worth up to $3,000. So plan your own stays for slower weeks.

Now risk tolerance. In 0.2, the five-year test added five years of cash flow to the sale proceeds. Then it compared that total with the $142,688 they put in. The base case came out $27,732 ahead before tax. The weak case came out $27,503 behind. I want both owners to look at that second number and say out loud whether they could live with it.

If the honest answer is no, that's a readiness result, not a failure.

slides.title: Maya and Chris would spend $155,302 before their first guest on the DSCR quote
rows: Cash to close (25% down, closing costs; DSCR includes 1 point)
slides.notes:
Now the full stack for Maya and Chris. Figures without a tag come from the course example file. The new ones are marked as assumptions.

Start with cash to close. On the DSCR quote that's $110,688: the $96,250 down payment plus $14,438 of closing costs, including one point of $2,888. On the conventional quote it's $107,800, because there's no point.

Then furnishing and setup, $32,000. A repair and safety punch list, $4,000. Inspections, including septic and specialists, $1,500. Permit and registration fees, $600. And two months of launch carrying costs. That's $6,514 on the DSCR quote and $6,368 on the conventional, because the payment is lower.

Add it up on the DSCR side: $110,688 plus $32,000, plus $4,000, plus $1,500, plus $600, plus $6,514. That's $155,302 spent before a single guest checks in. On the conventional side, $152,268.

Compare that with the $96,250 down payment we started with. And we haven't added either reserve yet. That's the next slide.

slides.title: Holding both reserves leaves them $11,644 short on DSCR and $8,172 on conventional
rows: Property reserve: 6 months PITIA, also their own target (assumption)

box.label: Two readings of the same table
box.text: **Lender's view:** $54,698 left after spending, about 21 months of PITIA. **Their plan:** they can't fund both reserves at once.

slides.notes:
Now add the two held layers.

Their household's essential spending is $8,500 a month, an assumption. They want to keep six months of it as their own emergency savings, $51,000. The property reserve is $15,342 on the DSCR quote. That's the lender figure, and it also covers their own target of $15,246 from the delay-plus-weak-year chart.

So the full stack on the DSCR quote is $155,302 plus $15,342 plus $51,000. That's $221,644. They have $210,000. The gap is $11,644. On the conventional quote the gap is $8,172.

Here's the part I want you to notice. There are two ways to read this table.

The lender's view: after spending $155,302, Maya and Chris would still hold $54,698. That's about 21 months of the DSCR payment, well above a six-month rule. On paper, a lender may say yes.

Their own plan: they can't fund the house's reserve and their own emergency savings at the same time. They're short.

This is the gap the down payment check hides.

slides.title: Close the gap with time first, then financing, price, and a phased furnishing plan
items: **Time.** Saving $3,500 a month closes the DSCR gap in about 3.3 months, the conventional gap in about 2.3.
**Financing.** The conventional quote needs $2,888 less at closing (no point), shrinking the gap to $8,172, if they qualify (PA.7).
**Price.** A lower price cuts the down payment and closing costs. PA.1 turns this into a hard cap.
**Furnishing plan.** A phased plan may cut the up-front budget, without cutting safety or listing accuracy (OP.6).

box.label: Don't do this
box.text: Shrink the emergency fund to make the table balance, or count a HELOC as savings.

slides.notes:
So what can close the gap? Here are the options in the order I'd look at them.

Time first. If Maya and Chris save $3,500 a month, which is an assumption, the DSCR gap closes in about 3.3 months. The conventional gap closes in about 2.3 months. Searching, underwriting, and closing take a while anyway, so time is often the cheapest fix.

Financing second. The conventional quote needs $2,888 less at closing, because it has no point. The payment is lower too, if they qualify. That shrinks the gap to $8,172. It doesn't close it. PA.7 compares the two loans.

Price third. A lower price reduces the down payment and closing costs. In PA.1 we turn this into a hard price cap.

Furnishing fourth. A phased furnishing plan may cut the up-front budget. OP.6 covers how to do that without cutting safety or listing accuracy.

And two things they should not do. Don't shrink the emergency fund to make the table balance. And don't count a HELOC as savings. Both of those make the table look fine and leave the household exposed.

slides.title: Score every line Green, Yellow, or Red before you shop, starting with cash

bands.d: Clears it only with a written condition and a date

slides.notes:
Here's the one-page readiness scorecard. Fill it in before you shop. Score each line Green, Yellow, or Red. There are 13 lines. This slide shows the first seven.

Line 1 is the full cash stack from liquid savings. Green is a surplus. Yellow is a gap you can close with normal saving within six months. Red is a bigger gap, or a stack that only works with borrowed money.

Line 2 is your emergency savings after closing. Six months or more is Green. Under three is Red.

Line 3 is the property reserve. Green means you meet the lender's rule and your own target.

Lines 4 to 6 are the lender lines. A verbal quote is Yellow, as long as written quotes are scheduled in PA.6 and PA.7. For line 6, ask for the maximum DTI or minimum coverage ratio in writing.

Line 7 is the delay test. Can the property reserve absorb three extra months without touching the family's fund?

If a lender figure isn't in writing yet, mark it "lender to confirm" with a date.

slides.title: The last six lines test time, involvement, personal use, and your nerve
rows: Hours exceed the plan, plus a local backup
Works only if you self-manage, and you're unsure
Fails with the model you'll use
Both accept the 5-year weak case in writing
Below the Pub 527 threshold, or CPA-reviewed
Compared owning with leasing (0.2); owning chosen for a reason
Leasing fits better and you'd still buy
slides.notes:
Here are lines 8 to 13.

Line 8 is the weak first season. Green means the property reserve covers the weak-case loss for two years or more. Under one year is Red.

Line 9 is time. Green means the hours you really have beat the plan's estimate, and you have a local backup for when you can't get there.

Line 10 tests your involvement choice. Does the deal still work with the management model you'll actually use? Yellow is the honest middle: it works only if you self-manage, and you're not sure you will.

Line 11 is risk tolerance. Green means both owners accept the five-year weak-case result, in writing. If either can't, it's Red.

Line 12 is personal use. Below the Publication 527 threshold, or reviewed by a CPA, is Green.

Line 13 asks whether you considered the lease path. Green means you compared owning with leasing in 0.2, and you chose owning for a stated reason. Red is when leasing clearly fits better and you'd buy anyway.

Be hard on yourself here. Nobody else sees this page.

bands.d: Clears it only with a written condition and a date

slides.title: Your scorecard sends you to PA.1, to financing first, to the lease path, or to wait
rows: **Wait.** Fix the time, risk, or personal-use question before money is at stake.
**Lease path (Part One).** The example apartment, Alder Street, needed $20,370 on day one.
One Red, on any of lines 3 to 8
**Improve financing or liquidity first.** Get written quotes, pay debt, or save. Rescore in 60 to 90 days.
No Reds; each Yellow has a written condition and date
**Proceed to PA.1 with conditions.** Each condition goes in your buy box: no offer until it's met.
No Reds, but a Yellow has no condition or date
**Wait.** Write the condition and date, then rescore.
slides.caption: Cut-offs and rescore timing are teaching defaults (assumption), not lender or industry rules.
slides.notes:
Here's what the scorecard tells you to do. Check the rows from the top, and stop at the first one that matches.

Two or more Reds anywhere: wait, and rescore in six months.

One Red on time, involvement, risk, or personal use: wait. Fix that question before money is at stake. If time is the only problem, check whether a co-host still leaves the deal positive.

One Red on cash, emergency savings, or the lease comparison: use the lease path from Part One. A lease needs far less cash. Alder Street, the course's example leased apartment, needed $20,370 on day one. Start with lesson 1.3.

One Red on lines 3 to 8: improve financing or liquidity first, and rescore in 60 to 90 days.

No Reds: if it's all Green, proceed to PA.1. If every Yellow has a written condition and a date, proceed with conditions. Each condition goes into your buy box. If a Yellow has no condition yet, write one and rescore.

These cut-offs are my teaching defaults, not lender or industry rules.
slides.keyline: Check the rows from top to bottom. The first row that matches decides.

slides.eyebrow: Maya and Chris, scored · Yellows first
slides.title: Maya and Chris have no Reds and four Yellows with conditions, so they proceed to PA.1
rows: Gap of $11,644 (DSCR) or $8,172. Save $3,500 a month; funded 4 months after starting PA.1
Hypothetical, verbal quotes only. Written quotes in PA.6 and PA.7, before any offer
About 2.7 hours a week; local backup not yet named. Name one in PA.1
Works only if they self-manage; untested. Loses $7,798 a year with an 18% co-host (0.2)
$9,771 for 3 months; reserve covers it with $5,571 left
$15,342 covers about 2.8 years of the $5,475 loss
Both reviewed the -$27,503 five-year weak case and accept it
10 days, below the 21.2-day threshold; CPA to confirm
slides.caption: Also Green: 2 (keep $51,000), 3 ($15,342 meets the lender rule and their $15,246 target), 4 and 6 (740 credit; 35.6% DTI, coverage 1.18 to 2.42; lender to confirm in writing), 13 (chose owning for a long hold).
slides.notes:
Here's how Maya and Chris scored. No Reds, and four Yellows.

Line 1, the cash stack: they're $11,644 short on the DSCR quote, or $8,172 on the conventional. Their condition is a funding date four months after they start PA.1, saving $3,500 a month. Line 5, lender fit: they only have hypothetical quotes, so written ones come in PA.6 and PA.7, before any offer. Line 9, time: they haven't named a local backup yet, so they name one in PA.1. Line 10, involvement: the deal only works if they self-manage, and they haven't tested that yet.

Everything else is Green. Their reserve meets the lender rule and their own $15,246 target. Credit and debt capacity are Green, with the lender to confirm in writing. Both of them accept being $27,503 behind in the weak case.

So the outcome is proceed to PA.1, with conditions. The saving runs while they work through the next few lessons, PA.2 to PA.4. And self-management becomes a hard requirement in their buy box.

slides.title: Your lender, CPA, insurer, and permit office each confirm a line of your stack
rows: Reserve months and how they're calculated, minimum credit score, down payment, acceptable sources of funds (HELOC, gifts, retirement), and how rental income is counted
Tax effect of retirement withdrawals, how your hours count for material participation, and how personal-use days are treated
The premium and when it's due, so layer 2 or layer 6 is accurate
Fees and processing time, so the launch carrying-cost assumption is realistic
slides.notes:
Here's who confirms what for your stack.

Each lender, in writing: the reserve months and how they calculate them, the minimum credit score, and the down payment. Also which sources of funds they accept, like HELOC money, gifts, or retirement assets. And how they count rental income. Ask every lender the same questions so you can compare the answers side by side.

Your CPA: the tax effect of any retirement withdrawal, how your hours count for material participation, and how personal-use days are treated.

Your insurance agent: the premium and when it's due. Depending on timing, it lands in closing costs or in launch carrying costs. Either way, it needs to be a real number.

The local permit office: the fees and the processing time. That's what tells you whether two months of launch carrying costs is realistic, or whether you need to plan for more.

Every one of these turns an assumption on your stack into a confirmed number. The more lines you confirm, the more you can trust your scorecard.

slides.title: Four short tasks produce your own cash stack and a scored readiness page
items: Total your liquid savings, leaving out retirement accounts and home equity.
Write your essential monthly spending and multiply by the months of emergency savings you'll keep.
Fill in the eight-layer stack for one realistic price. Use Maya and Chris's lines as marked placeholders until you have your own.
Score all 13 lines of the readiness scorecard, with evidence, and pick your outcome.
slides.next: Next: **PA.1, Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box (Market, Property Type, Price Range, Goals).** Lease path? Go to lesson 1.3. Wait? Set a rescore date now.
slides.notes:
Four tasks. The first two take minutes. The stack takes longer until you have lender numbers.

First, total your liquid savings. Leave out retirement accounts. Leave out home equity. That's the number you work with.

Second, write down your household's essential monthly spending, and decide how many months you'll keep as emergency savings. Multiply. That money is off the table for the house.

Third, fill in the eight-layer stack for one realistic price. Where you don't have a number yet, use Maya and Chris's line and mark it as an assumption. Scale it to your price where it's a percentage, like the down payment. Then replace each one using the who-confirms-what list. Write down the surplus or the gap.

Fourth, score all 13 lines, with evidence, and read off your outcome.

If your scorecard says proceed, go to PA.1, Discovery: Defining Your Buy Box. It turns your goals and numbers into a written search specification. If it said lease path, go to Part One, lesson 1.3. If it said wait, put a rescore date on your calendar today.

slides.notes:
Here are the sources.

Fannie Mae's Selling Guide section B3-4.1-01 backs the reserve points. Reserves are counted in months of PITIA. There's no minimum for a principal residence, and other financed properties can add more. One honest note: the exact month count for an investment property wasn't shown in what I could check. That's why the 6 months on these slides is an assumption.

Section B3-3.8-03 is Fannie Mae's section on short-term rental income. Confirm the current version with your lender. Kiavi's DSCR guide backs the point that one lender looks at credit and down payment too. That's one lender, not a standard.

The CFPB page backs the HELOC points: variable rate, and your home as collateral.

IRS Publications 925 and 527 back the participation and personal-use points.

Every Cedar Ridge figure is an assumption from the course file. The new ones listed on the slide are assumptions too. Replace each one with your own number as soon as you have it.
